title: TB7-18416

Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (the principal Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXXthe associate Appellant), citizens of Nepal, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated September 7, 2017, rejecting their claim(s) for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the principal Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXXthe associate Appellant), citizens of Nepal, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated September 7, 2017, rejecting their claim(s) for refugee protection. The Appellants have submitted new evidence with the appeal as referred to in subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA),1 and request an oral hearing be held pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.

The details of the claims are provided in the narrative of the Appellants' Basis of Claim (BOC) forms. They allege that they fear persecution and fear that Maoists will abduct, physically harm, or kill them because of a failure to support them or comply with their demands, as well as the principal Appellant's long time support of the Nepali Congress Party (NCP). They allege that Maoists began demanding "donations" in 2001. The demands escalated and resulted in three abductions where death threats were made should they not comply with the increasing demands for money. The last abduction took place in September 2015. The Appellants fled Nepal in XXXX 2015.

The Appellants' hearing for refugee protection was held on August 24, 2017. In a decision on September 7, 2017, the RPD rejected the Appellants' claim finding that they had a viable Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Kathmandu, Nepal. The Appellants submit that the RPD erred in its assessment of the IFA location because the Maoists have a nationwide network.

For questions of fact, mixed fact and law, the RAD has applied the standard of correctness as per Huruglica. In assessing issues involving credibility of oral testimony, I may apply the RAD modified standard of reasonableness in those situations where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage as per the decision in X (Re), 2017 CanLII 33034 (CA IRB). ADMISSIBILITY OF NEW EVIDENCE PRESENTED ON APPEAL
In support of this appeal, the Appellants submitted a personal affidavit and a Maoist Threat Letter, along with the courier envelope,2 as proposed new evidence.

Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the Appellants may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected3 in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection. It is for the Appellants to make full and detailed submissions in their Memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) and how that evidence relates to the Appellants.4

In addition, if the new evidence meets one of the explicit legislative factors in subsection 110(4), then the second step of the analysis is for the RAD to apply the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh.5 In Singh, the Federal Court of Appeal held that the RAD should assess the admissibility of the new evidence for its credibility, relevance and newness. The RAD is not to consider the fourth Raza factor of materiality to the admission of new evidence, which is a consideration for subsection 110(6) and the request for an oral hearing.6

The RAD has reviewed the principal Appellant's personal affidavit document7 and notes that it provides a statement indicating that his brother who lives in Kathmandu called him and stated that three Maoists came to his home and gave him a letter indicating that they are looking for the principal Appellant and his wife. The Maoists threatened his brother, telling him not to go to the police. The RAD finds the affidavit arose after the rejection of the Appellants' claim and meets the basic requirements of subsection 110(4); it will be assessed applying the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh.8

As well, the RAD has reviewed the Maoist Threat Letter9 dated October 2, 2017, which indicates it arose following the rejection of the Appellants' claim, meeting the basic requirements of subsection 110(4). The RAD must further assess the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh, where the Federal Court of Appeal held that the RAD should assess the admissibility of the new evidence for its credibility, relevance and newness. The RAD notes on its review of the evidence in the record that all of the Appellants' problems with the Maoists occurred in their home and are with a separatist Maoist faction (a splinter group10) described as the Biplav faction (Netra Bikram Chand Biplav).

The documentary evidence states that a faction of Maoists led by Mohan Baidya [Vaidya] split from the UCPN-M in 2012 to create the Maoist NCP-M. Baidya was described as a "communist hard-liner" leading a "dissenting faction of the ruling Maoist party." Nekram Bikram Chandra was the Secretary of this faction, which became known as the CPN-M. A further split in the Baidya faction in 2014 led to the formation of the Biplav or Biplab faction of the CPN-M, which became known as the CPN-Biplav or Chand faction.11

The RAD notes the documentary evidence indicates that this group, composed of former, frustrated combatants and other factions that have rejected accommodation with the elected government,12 is involved in criminal activity and extortion.

The RAD notes the following: * The letter indicates that it is issued by the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist), Area 3, but it does not provide any further information to identify where it arose from or whether there is any association with the Biplav group that the Appellants allege are the agents of persecution. * The letterhead is of simple design and could be produced by any individual with basic word-processing skills and a printer. * The letter is hand-filled, with no security features beyond a signature from someone who describes themselves as "In Charge."

The RAD finds the documentary evidence indicates that since the 2006 Comprehensive Peace Agreement, "CPN-M, UCPN [and] YCL have stopped issuing threat letters," because they have been part of the democratic process and government since then, and because human rights groups and the media monitor political parties and their activities, including the Maoists, which makes sending threat letters "a political blunder." The documentary evidence carries on to note that there are no cases of the issuance of threat letters currently by the CPN-M, UCPN, and YCL. Threat letters were a "widespread" practice during the conflict between 1996 and 2006, and then a "few" were issued during the peace process between 2006 and 2009. After 2009, INSEC has documented "some cases of oral threats and beatings," but is not aware of cases of threat letters issued by Maoist groups since 2010." Another NGO, the AHRC, stated that the UCPN, CPN-M and YCL did issue threat letters before 2006, but was not aware of any cases of such threat letters being issued after these parties joined "mainstream politics."

The RAD finds the documentary evidence indicates that letters such as that submitted as new evidence are not utilized in the current environment in Nepal, and that they have not been seen by any of the agencies referred to in the evidence for some time. The documentary evidence further states that the AHRC has come across "a lot of forgery cases" where people have obtained letters speaking about "threats and demands." The AHRC representative also noted that in Nepal, one can "easily" design a letterhead and a stamp for less than US$5 at any "designing outlet."13

The RAD further notes that the prevalence of fraudulent documents does not mean that every single "Threat Letter" document is necessarily false. However, the RAD finds in the context of all of the concerns noted above, that it must consider this document with caution.

The RAD notes that the last event involving the Appellants occurred in September 2015. The RPD issued its decision in September 2017, clearly stating that there had been no action by the Maoists for an extended period of time, noting that the principal Appellant's brother and the Appellants' son lived in Kathmandu without any interaction or problems from Maoists. It seems unusual that there would be no response or actions by the Maoists to seek out the Appellants or their family members for two years, and then shortly following the RPD decision, the Maoists appear at the Appellant's brother's home in Kathmandu and leave a letter threatening the Appellants.

The RAD finds that it is too much of a coincidence that mere days after the issuance of a negative decision in this claim, the Maoists suddenly reappeared seeking the Appellants. With regard to this coincidence, the RAD is guided by the Federal Court decision in Ankrah,14 where J. Noel stated: The applicant's story does otherwise reveal a series of events of chance, and it was open to the tribunal to conclude therefrom that the Applicant's testimony was too fortuitous in nature to be believed.

The RAD has additionally considered the decision in Meng where the Court held that: [22] ...the Board's remark that the timing of the alleged church raid is an "extraordinary coincidence" that is suspiciously convenient is not unreasonable in light of the evidence, notably the fact that they were visiting their sister in Canada and their visitor visa was set to expire. Although I agree with the Applicants that there is nothing inherently implausible about a church raid occurring while the Applicants were away, there are a number of suspicious aspects to the timing of their story.15

The RAD finds that is not unreasonable to infer that the coincidence of the timing of the events is improbable and that the renewed actions by the Maoists was not a coincidence, but a carefully concocted addition to enhance the appeal and to bolster the authenticity of the story. The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that this coincidence is a reasonable cause to assign little probative value to the events described in the principal Appellant's affidavit and finds it is not credible.

The RAD further finds that upon a review of all of the findings in respect to the Appellants' "Threat Letter," there is an evidentiary basis to undermine its credibility and assign no evidentiary weight to the document.
The RAD finds the new evidence does not meet the credibility requirements of the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh16 and the documents will not be admitted as new evidence in this appeal.

The RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in subsection 110(3) of the IRPA that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal, is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim, and, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.17

The Appellants have submitted no admissible new evidence in support of their appeal. As such, the RAD must proceed without a hearing on the basis of the RPD's record; the application for an oral hearing is denied.

The RPD found the determinative issue is the availability of an IFA in Kathmandu, Nepal. The Appellants argue that: 1. Kathmandu is XXXX XXXX from the Appellants' home area where they have encountered their past problems with the Maoists. 2. The Maoists have a nationwide network and operate throughout the country. 3. The Maoists are currently the ruling party in Nepal, and that the agents of persecution in this case are, therefore, effectively state actors. Given that the Maoists hold power at the highest level of the Nepali government, and the government is ubiquitous in Nepal, it defies reason to suggest that the Appellants have an IFA anywhere in the country. 4. The Maoists have continued to visit the principal Appellant's parents inXXXX XXXX (they have returned on 3-4 occasions since the Appellants left Nepal) and insist that they are intent on finding and killing the Appellants, demonstrating the extent to which the agents of persecution have maintained their desire and resolve to locate and harm the Appellants.

In assessing an IFA, the RAD must apply a two-pronged test cited in the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Rasaratnam:18 1) the Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA. 2) moreover, the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for the claimant to seek refuge there.

Both prongs must be satisfied to find that the Appellants have an IFA. Once the issue of IFA has been raised and the potential IFAs have been identified, the burden of proof rests with the Appellants to show that they do not have an IFA. The finding of an IFA must be based on a distinct evaluation of a region for that purpose taking into account the Appellants' identities. An IFA must be a realistic and attainable option. The Appellants cannot be required to encounter great physical danger or to undergo undue hardship in traveling there or staying there.19

While an analysis of whether a particular appellant faces a serious possibility of persecution in the proposed IFA under the first prong of the Rasaratnam test is necessarily fact-specific, the RAD is aware that as a general principle, Canadian courts have held that large urban areas cannot be assumed to be an IFA by virtue of their population size alone,20 and that the distance between the proposed IFA and the location of the persecutors does not in itself serve to establish that the proposed IFA is viable.21 That said, the IFA need not be far away from where the appellant has previously lived: the concept of an IFA does not require that the safe haven be in another city or province than the place of origin so long as it is truly an area in which the appellant can seek refuge from the persecution experienced in their home district.22 Ultimately, the question of whether an appellant has shown, on a balance of probabilities, that they face a serious possibility of persecution in the proposed IFA will turn on their evidence, keeping in mind the general principles above. First Prong Proximity of the IFA

The RPD found that despite the distance between the Appellants' village and Kathmandu (XXXX XXXX according to the principal Appellant), they have a viable IFA in Kathmandu. The Appellants submit that they were only 80-90 kilometres from Kathmandu when they had their last encounter with the Maoists. Additionally, the principal Appellant testified that the Maoists told them they have people in every part of the country.

The RAD has discussed the Appellants' statements about the ability of the Maoists to locate them anywhere in the country previously and found it was grounded in speculation. The RAD has also confirmed the RPD finding that there is a lack of objective evidence supporting close ties, coordination, and communication between the Maoist faction in their home district and other Maoist groups throughout the country, including the capital city of Kathmandu.

The RAD further notes that the principal Appellant confirmed in his statements in his BOC, as well as in his testimony, that in September 2015, at the time they were stopped in Mugline, they were still in their local district going about their regular process of delivering fruit to customers. The RAD finds that the statements indicate the local Maoist group did not stop them that day because they were attempting to flee the area, but because they were simply trying to extort more money from them. The RAD finds the Appellants' submissions are insufficient to support that this particular action provides persuasive evidence that the Maoists can locate them in the proposed IFA.
The RAD agrees with the finding of the RPD in this issue and the Appellants' argument fails. The Profile of the Agent of Persecution

The Appellants submit the Maoists are currently the ruling party in Nepal, and that the agents of persecution in this case are, therefore, effectively state actors. The Appellants further argue that the Maoists hold power at the highest level of the Nepali government, and the government is ubiquitous in Nepal, therefore, it defies reason to suggest that the Appellants have an IFA anywhere in the country. The RAD is not persuaded by the argument of the Appellants.

The RAD notes that the documentary evidence describes the Maoists in Nepal as a series of groups with various fragments or splinter offshoots. The documentary evidence states that "some of these groups are part of the government, while others are opposed to the government and are engaged in boycotts and violent activities."23 [citation omitted] The documentary evidence notes: "[t]here are a number of Maoist factions who have rejected accommodation with the elected government and continue political activity beyond the mainstream Maoist party," elements of which may be involved in extortion. [citation omitted] The evidence carries on to note: ...that instances of kidnapping and extortion by Maoist groups "are increasingly rare occurrences from a political party perspective" and are "not common any longer"... The same source indicated that "organized human rights violations/abuses are not taking place in Nepal due to the Maoist party," although there may be involvement in some criminal activities by "former, frustrated combatants in certain parts of Nepal." 24 [citation omitted]

The RAD finds that many of these splinter groups have broken away from the central "Maoist" identity and values. The RAD notes, as discussed previously, that all of the Appellants' problems with the Maoists occurred in their home area with a separatist Maoist faction (a splinter group) described as the Biplav faction (Netra Bikram Chand Biplav).25

The documentary evidence indicates that this group, composed of former, frustrated combatants and other factions that have rejected accommodation with the elected government,26 is involved in criminal activity and extortion. The documentary evidence further confirms that the Unified Communist Party or Nepal-Maoists that joined the peace process in April 2006 has since split into five groups, one of which is the dissident Biplav's group.27

The evidence notes that in 2016, the Biplav Maoists formed an independent local council in the XXXX area, stating that it would defy the structures of the present government and would implement the constitution made by the party.28 The RAD finds the documentary evidence indicates that the Biplav faction is a dissident group operating outside of the ruling government. They engage in extortion mainly outside of Kathmandu in the Mid-West and Far-West regions of Nepal.29 The RAD notes that the evidence demonstrates that these groups are considered violent, but it does not demonstrate that they have any influence or control over the current ruling government in Nepal.

The RAD further notes that while a few articles indicate the Maoist groups may be involved in activities in Kathmandu, the evidence does not indicate that they have been active in extortion and kidnapping of individuals with a profile similar to the Appellants in Kathmandu.

The RAD finds that the agent of persecution seeking the Appellants is a dissident faction of the larger grouping of organizations identified as "Maoists" in Nepal. The RAD has reviewed the Appellants' testimony and documentary evidence relating to these numerous groups in Nepal. The RAD notes the Appellants' evidence clearly identifies a local Maoist group of the Biplav faction as the agents of persecution. The RAD finds there is little persuasive evidence to allow it to find that the Biplav faction has any direct linkage to the ruling groups in Nepal.
The RAD finds this aspect of the Appellants' argument must fail. The Ability of the Agent of Persecution to Communicate Throughout Nepal

The RAD has considered if the Appellants will face risk in relocating to Kathmandu due to their profile as individuals who were being sought for extortion by their local Biplav Maoist group. The RPD found that the objective evidence provides limited support to the Appellants' assertion that the Maoists have a nationwide network and operate throughout the country; further, it found little evidence to demonstrate the strength of the connections between regions within the larger Maoist network. The Appellant submits that the evidence confirms the Maoists have a nationwide network, giving them the ability to find them anywhere in Nepal. The Appellants further submit that the RPD as well as the documentary evidence confirm this fact. The RAD is not persuaded by the argument of the Appellant.

The RAD notes the principal Appellant was asked how he knew that the Maoists network would be able to able to find him and his wife. He answered that he was not clear how they operate, but he knew that they have a large network to find them. He was asked to explain how he was aware of this information and testified that this was what he had heard, further stating that he had no personal knowledge of anyone who had experienced problems with the Maoists. The RAD finds the Appellants' explanation provides little support for his allegations regarding the communication ability of the agent of persecution and that it is based on speculation.

The RAD has reviewed the documentary evidence before the RPD, which includes both the Board's National Documentation Package (NDP) and the Appellant's documentary evidence. The RAD finds that the Board's objective evidence makes a statement that the Young Communist League (YCL), a youth offshoot of the Maoist party, has a "nationwide network,"30 but beyond that, the detailed information in this document addressing the actions of the YCL towards those associated with opposing political views provides no additional information about the ability of various divisions to communicate and share information throughout the country. The RAD further notes that the documentary evidence does not confirm any linkage between the YCL and the Biplav Maoists. Nor does it make any mention of the ability of the numerous Maoist factions to communicate with each other or whether they would have any interest in sharing information due to their opposing political viewpoints. The RAD's review of the documentary evidence finds little evidence to demonstrate the strength of the connections between regions within the large number of Maoist groups, and if/how the different regions coordinate and share information, including in circumstances such as the Appellants.'

The RAD additionally notes that much of Nepal's communication infrastructure was destroyed in the 2015 earthquake. The country's telephone communication system is described as "poor," its mobile- cellular network is described as "fair," and internet penetration is 17.6 percent of the population.31 The RAD finds the documentary evidence confirms that communication is limited. The RAD finds the singular statement in the documentary evidence, as well as the Appellants' statements about the Maoist "network," are vague and non-specific, and they are not supported by any additional evidence before the RAD.

The RAD finds on its review of all of the evidence, that there is insufficient persuasive evidence to support the Appellant's allegations that the Biplav Maoists have an ability to communicate throughout Nepal in order to locate the Appellant. The RAD supports the findings of the RPD in this issue and the Appellants' argument must fail. The Appellants' Family Members

The RPD found that the fact that the local Maoist group had not sought out the principal Appellant's brother or son living in Kathmandu during the past two years in an attempt to locate the Appellants, supported the viability of the IFA. The RPD further found that the Appellants' testimony confirmed that the brother, who is an NCP supporter like the Appellants, and their son, the child of an NCP supporter, have not reported any problems with Maoists in Kathmandu. The Appellants submit that the new evidence submitted in support of their appeal refutes the RPD finding.

The RAD notes the new evidence relied on by the Appellants was assessed earlier in this decision and it was found not to be credible. The RAD did not admit this evidence in this appeal. As such, the Appellants' arguments arising from the letter are unable to demonstrate that the RPD erred.

The RAD further notes the Appellants have not contested the RPD's finding in respect to the brother or the Appellants' son experiencing no problems from any Maoist factions in Kathmandu because of their association with the NCP. The RAD supports the RPD findings in this issue and finds the Appellants' argument that they have provided persuasive evidence that the local Maoist group has sought out the principal Appellant's brother and son living in Kathmandu in an attempt to locate the Appellants, and that this impacts the RPD's IFA finding, must fail.

The RAD has reviewed the available documentary evidence as well as the audio recording of the hearing. The RAD notes that in order to target the Appellants in Kathmandu, the Biplav Maoists from the Appellants' home area would be required to: 1) Learn the Appellants have returned to Nepal; 2) Learn the Appellants have relocated to Kathmandu; and, 3) Determine the whereabouts of the Appellants in the city. The RAD finds it reasonable to expect that if an individual or group had sufficient resources to be able to learn of a person's return to Nepal, and their presence in any area in Nepal, there would be objective evidence to support this.

The RAD finds there is not enough sufficient credible evidence to establish that the agent of persecution has the operational capacity or geographic reach to learn of the Appellants' return to Nepal upon arrival at a regular port of entry to the country, or trace the Appellants' movements within Nepal.

The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, as did the RPD, that there is no serious possibility that Maoists in Kathmandu will target the Appellants based on their real or perceived political opinions (i.e. as NCP members or supporters). In addition, the RAD finds that the Appellants have not advanced sufficient persuasive evidence that there is a serious possibility that the Biplav Maoists from their local area have the ability to locate the Appellants in Kathmandu. Second Prong

The RPD found that when it considered the Appellants' particular circumstances, it was objectively reasonable for them to reside in Kathmandu. The principal Appellant stated that the family would be able to survive if the Maoists were not targeting them. The RAD notes that the Appellants did not advance any additional testimony or provide reasons in their Memorandum as to why they would not be able to reside in the proposed IFA location. The RAD notes: * The principal Appellant has twelve years of education, which includes some university education.32 * The principal Appellant has extensive work experience as both a XXXX and a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.33 * The associate Appellant has worked as a XXXX person in Nepal.34 * The principal Appellant has a brother in Kathmandu who would likely be available to assist the Appellants in their relocation. * The principal Appellant testified that they did not face any barriers to finding employment or housing in Kathmandu. * The Appellants provided testimony to indicate that they had relocated in Nepal on a previous occasion. * The Appellants are experienced international travellers. They have travelled to Canada and resettled without reporting any significant problems.

The RAD finds after a review of all of the evidence, that given the Appellants' personal circumstances, it is not unduly harsh or objectively unreasonable for the Appellants to relocate to Kathmandu in Nepal. Conclusions on IFA

Upon review of the appeal record, including the testimony of the Appellants, their documentary evidence and the information available in the NDP, the RAD agrees with the conclusion of the RPD for the same reasons,35 that Kathmandu offers the Appellants a viable IFA within Nepal; the claim therefore fails on this basis.

Once the IFA has been named, the burden is on the Appellants to show that either of the two prongs of the Rasaratnam test are not met. There is insufficient evidence in the record to suggest that the Biplav Maoists from their home region would have the reach or influence to locate the Appellants elsewhere in Nepal, including specifically in Kathmandu. The RAD further finds that they would not be able to enlist other Maoist factions to conduct a national search for the Appellants, such that it would give rise to a serious possibility of persecution or subject them personally to a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture. Likewise, they have not demonstrated that in their personal circumstances, the proposed IFA would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh. As noted above, the burden of proof rests with the Appellant to show that they do not have an IFA to Kathmandu once raised, and the RAD finds that the Appellants have not discharged that burden.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.
